newsitem.title: UK: Unilever chief warns Britain against EMU opt-out.
newsitem.headline: Unilever chief warns Britain against EMU opt-out.

text.p: The chairman of Anglo-Dutch consumer products giant Unilever said the company might review its investments in Britain if the government fails to join European Monetary Union, Wednesday's Guardian newspaper said.

Niall FitzGerald, chairman of Unilever's British arm, said he had misgivings about the timetable set for monetary union, but said it "was not a matter in which Britain could sit on the sidelines hurling abuse", the Guardian said.

"If Britain absented itself, that would certainly lead to reconsideration of certain investment decisions. If the UK was gently floated off into the Atlantic, we'd have to reconsider things," the Guardian quoted FitzGerald as saying.

FitzGerald's comments echo a warning by the Japanese motor company Toyota that it would reconsider its future investments in Britain if London did not join the European single currency, planned to be issued from 1999.

Those remarks by Toyota President Hiroshi Okuda struck a raw nerve in Britain, where the government has taken great pride in attracting foreign investment and believes it has done so by refusing to sign up to European Union policies affecting employment laws.

Prime Minister John Major, who must call a general election by May, he has been relying on an economic recovery to boost his slim chances of being re-elected. His Conservative Party is lagging opposition Labour by around 20 points in opinion polls.
Both Labour and the Conservatives have refused to commit themselves to signing up to a single currency.
If Unilever were to shift its investments away from Britain, it could cause serious hardship. The company employs 21,000 people in Britain and in some areas it is the main employer.
The Guardian said that FitzGerald was speaking on Tuesday after Unilever announced a 15 percent rise in profit and said it planned to sell its specialty chemicals business.
